nodes.title: Nonsingular binary blocks
nodes.statement: On F² set [a,b](x,y)=a x²+xy+b y². Its polar matrix is [[2a,1],[1,2b]]; it is nonsingular exactly when 1−4ab≠0. Throughout, nonsingular means that the polar bilinear map has zero kernel; for these even spaces it agrees with Mathlib Nondegenerate. The hyperbolic plane is xy, including in characteristic two.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: Use the existing quadratic-map sum and scalar actions on coordinate monomials. Compute the polar matrix and its determinant.

acceptance: [1,1] over F₂ is anisotropic and nonsingular.

nodes.title: Witt cancellation and splitting in characteristic two
nodes.statement: For finite-dimensional nonsingular quadratic spaces over a field, split off hyperbolic planes until the complement is anisotropic. The anisotropic complement and Witt index are unique up to isometry; cancellation holds for an orthogonal nonsingular summand. Extend the existing odd-characteristic theorems to characteristic two, using xy for the hyperbolic plane.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: For an isotropic vector v choose w with polar(v,w)=1 and replace w by w−q(w)v, splitting an xy plane.

For cancellation extend an isometry of the common nonsingular subspace by the Witt extension argument, then restrict to its orthogonal complement. Iterate and compare maximal hyperbolic summands. The characteristic-two proof uses binary symplectic blocks, not division by 2.
acceptance: Dimension 2m and Witt index m characterize hyperbolicity.
No new odd-characteristic Witt decomposition is claimed.

nodes.statement: In characteristic two construct W_b(F), the Grothendieck ring of nonsingular symmetric bilinear spaces modulo metabolic classes; addition is orthogonal sum and multiplication is tensor product. nodes.title: Quadratic Witt module and bilinear tensor action
nodes.statement: Construct I_q(F), the group of even-dimensional nonsingular quadratic spaces modulo hyperbolic spaces, with its W_b(F)-module action. For a symmetric bilinear form b and q, define b⊗q by its quadratic polynomial and the rule (b⊗q)(w⊗v)=b(w,w)q(v); its polar form is b⊗polar(q). The tensor is nonsingular when b and q are. A metabolic b or hyperbolic q acts by a hyperbolic tensor. Equal Witt class plus equal dimension implies isometry. For char≠2 identify I_q with the fundamental ideal of the imported Witt ring.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: Define the polynomial tensor including the mixed terms fixed by its polar form; the pure-tensor formula alone is supplemented by those quadratic identities.
A lagrangian tensored with the other space gives the required hyperbolic dimension. Thus the action descends through metabolic and hyperbolic classes.
Use Witt cancellation to compare representatives of equal class and dimension; use polarization for the odd-characteristic ideal identification.
acceptance: The characteristic-two quadratic group is a module, with no unjustified product of two quadratic forms.
Tensoring the bilinear line ⟨c⟩_b scales q by c.

nodes.title: All-characteristic quadratic Pfister forms
nodes.statement: For n≥1 define an n-fold quadratic Pfister form as an (n−1)-fold bilinear Pfister tensor with a quadratic étale norm form. In char 2 its slots are a₁,…,a_(n−1)∈F× and a₀∈F, and its last factor is [1,a₀]; outer factors are ⟨1,−aᵢ⟩_b. In char≠2 use the existing n-fold parent construction with last factor ⟨1,−a₀⟩, a₀∈F×. The dimension is 2^n, the form represents 1, and its class belongs to I_q^n. Scaled n-fold forms generate I_q^n; unscaled forms generate additively for n>1. Do not assert the latter for n=1.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: In characteristic two iterate the bilinear tensor action on the binary last factor. Bilinear Pfister forms themselves are diagonal tensors, so no characteristic-two diagonal quadratic carrier is substituted.
Prove the dimension and represented unit by tensor bases. Binary-block decomposition and I_b generation give scaled Pfister generation; the difference identity (9.5) removes scalars for n>1.
For odd characteristic reuse the parent pfisterForm and its generation theorem. Compare [1,a] with ⟨1,−(1−4a)⟩ when 1−4a≠0 by completing the square.
acceptance: Zero terminal parameter in characteristic two gives a hyperbolic form.
The empty outer list gives the binary norm form, never a one-dimensional quadratic form.

nodes.title: Roundness of quadratic étale norms
nodes.statement: The norm form of a quadratic étale F-algebra is round: its nonzero represented values equal its similarity factors. In char 2 the algebra F[t]/(t²+t+a) has norm [1,a]; in char≠2 F[t]/(t²−a) has norm ⟨1,−a⟩. The split algebra gives the hyperbolic case.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: Multiplication by an element of nonzero norm is an invertible linear similarity, so represented units are similarity factors.
A norm form represents 1, so any similarity factor is represented. This proof also applies to the split étale algebra.
acceptance: Over F₂, [1,1] is the norm of F₄/F₂.
Represented values and similarity factors here range over F×.

nodes.title: The Pfister roundness induction step
nodes.statement: If ρ is nonsingular and round then ⟨1,−a⟩_b⊗ρ is round, for a∈F×. Its isotropy, hyperbolicity and the condition a∈D(ρ) are equivalent. This includes an isotropic round ρ: it is universal, so every a is represented and every such tensor is hyperbolic.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: Write a represented value as ρ(v)−aρ(w). Use roundness to normalize nonzero block values and the binary norm identity to obtain a similarity of the tensor.

If ρ is anisotropic, an isotropic vector of ρ⊥−aρ gives two nonzero represented values with ratio a. Roundness then identifies aρ with ρ, so the tensor is isometric to ρ⊥−ρ and is hyperbolic. If ρ is isotropic, nonsingularity splits off a hyperbolic plane, hence D(ρ)=F×. Roundness gives G(ρ)=F× and the same tensor identity; it does not require ρ itself to be hyperbolic.

nodes.title: The Cassels–Pfister polynomial representation theorem
nodes.statement: For anisotropic q over F and h∈F[t] nonzero, if q represents h over F(t), there is a polynomial vector w∈V[t] with q(w)=h. More precisely, for s∈V and an existing v∈V(F(t)) such that q(v) and polar(q)(s,v) both lie in F[t], one can choose w∈V[t] retaining both values.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.

nodes.title: The representation theorem for anisotropic forms
nodes.statement: For anisotropic q,ψ over F, dim ψ=m, the following are equivalent: D(ψ_E)⊆D(q_E) for every extension E/F; the generic polynomial ψ(T) is represented by q_F(T); ψ admits an injective isometry into q. Consequently dim ψ≤dim q.

proofSteps: Choose the quadratic normal form of ψ: nonsingular binary blocks together with a diagonal polar-radical part in characteristic two, or a diagonal form in odd characteristic (EKM7.29–7.31). nodes.title: Springer odd-degree preservation
nodes.statement: An anisotropic quadratic form remains anisotropic under every finite extension of odd degree, in all characteristics. Hence restriction on I_q is injective for such extensions.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.

Anisotropy over F makes q(v) nonzero of degree 2d, where d is the largest coordinate degree. Write q(v)=p·g. Then deg g=2d−n is nonnegative, odd and <n. An odd-degree irreducible factor h of g exists. Primitivity makes v modulo h nonzero, so it is an isotropic vector over F[t]/(h), contradicting minimality. This also covers inseparable simple extensions.

nodes.title: The quadratic similarity theorem
nodes.statement: For nonsingular even-dimensional q over F and nonzero f∈F[T], there exists a∈F× such that af is a similarity factor of q_F(T) iff q_F(p) is hyperbolic for every irreducible divisor p occurring oddly in f. hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: Necessity is odd-divisor specialization. For one variable a monic irreducible p is the norm of t−θ from its residue field extended by t. Hyperbolicity makes t−θ a similarity factor upstairs, and the similarity norm principle supplies p downstairs. Products and square factors reduce the general polynomial to irreducible factors.

For the multivariable induction take f irreducible of positive first-variable degree, set E=F(T′), and let g∈F[T′] be its leading coefficient. Gauss’s lemma makes f/g monic irreducible in E[t₁]; its residue field is F(f). The one-variable argument gives f/g, hence fg, as a similarity factor over F(T).

For an irreducible p of odd multiplicity in g, irreducibility of f gives p∤f. Apply the already proved necessity to the similarity factor fg: q is hyperbolic over F(p)(t₁). Pure-transcendental Witt injectivity descends this to F(p). Induct on g in fewer variables to get g*·g; multiplying by f/g gives f*·f, since g*=f*.

nodes.title: Vanishing for the kernel of the Milnor map
nodes.statement: In Morel’s induction fix N>0 and perfect k of characteristic ≠2. Assume s_n is an isomorphism for all fields over k in weights n<N, s_n(k) is an isomorphism for n≤N, and cup with τ=−1 makes H^(n−1)(F,Z/2(n−1))→H^(n−1)(F,Z/2(n)) surjective for every finite-type F/k and 1≤n<N. Then Ext^a_Ab(Sm_k,Zar)(k_n,j_N)=0 for 0≤n<N and a=0,1,2.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: The Rost cycle-module kernel has the lower-weight vanishing required by Morel3.10. Its contraction values at k vanish by the prime-field induction assumptions.
Model motivic complexes by equidimensional-cycle complexes. Remove cycle supports in X×A^n; the explicit A¹ translation homotopy gives derived Hom(Z/2(n),j_N[*])=0 in the needed weight range.

The universal-coefficient spectral sequence with top homology k_n gives Ext⁰ and Ext¹ zero. The τ-surjectivity makes the next Hom group inject into Hom(k_(n−1),j_N)=0, giving Ext². For n=0 use 0→Z→Z→k_0→0 and j_N(k)=0.

nodes.title: The Milnor conjecture for the quadratic Witt ring
nodes.statement: For every field F of characteristic ≠2 and every n≥0 the Milnor homomorphism s_n:K_n^M(F)/2→I(F)^n/I(F)^(n+1) is an isomorphism, naturally in F. Composing its inverse with the separately imported norm-residue isomorphism gives I_q^n/I_q^(n+1)≅H_q^n(F) for n≥1.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: Choose the prime field k, whose quadratic Milnor comparison is computed directly from finite-field Witt classes and the rational-field arithmetic residue sequence. The precise prime-field computation is included in the recorded Morel proof-input gap until its primary source is audited.
The motivic/étale norm-residue comparison gives τ-surjectivity. Use the kernel Ext vanishing to lift 0→i_N→W/I^(N+1)→W/I^N→0 to an extension by k_N.

The Witt presentation by units and relations on opens of tori lifts W to this extension. Its restriction to I^N kills I^(N+1) and sends an N-fold Pfister form to its symbol, giving a left inverse to s_N. Induct on N and pass to general field extensions by the supplied limit results.

Use norm residue only after the quadratic comparison. For characteristic zero OVV4.1 supplies an independent route; its standing characteristic-zero assumption is not extended to positive characteristic.
acceptance: Two distinct deep inputs remain visible: quadratic Witt comparison and norm residue.
Odd positive characteristic is covered by Morel, not by applying OVV4.1 outside its hypotheses.

nodes.statement: For char F=2 and n≥1 there is a natural additive isomorphism ē_n:I_q^n(F)/I_q^(n+1)(F)→H¹_et(F,Ω^(n−1)_log). nodes.statement: For a nonsingular quadratic n-fold Pfister form ρ, n≥1, define e_n(ρ)=ē_n([ρ] mod I_q^(n+1))∈H_q^n(F), using the odd-characteristic comparison followed by norm residue or the characteristic-two Kato comparison. It depends only on the isometry class. In odd characteristic it is the cup of the outer Kummer symbols with the final quadratic étale character; in characteristic two the last character is Artin–Schreier.

proofSteps: Take the quotient class under the existing Witt-class map and apply the appropriate comparison. Thus isometry invariance follows without defining the invariant by an unproved relation on slot tuples.
Evaluate on Pfister generators using the symbol formulas of the two comparisons.

nodes.title: The invariant-zero isotropy criterion
nodes.statement: For a quadratic n-fold Pfister form ρ, n≥1, e_n(ρ)=0 iff ρ is isotropic iff ρ is hyperbolic. This holds over every field in the H_q convention.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.

Conversely isotropy gives hyperbolicity and zero Witt class, so the invariant vanishes.

nodes.title: Unit Pfister reduction over henselian fields
nodes.statement: Let w be a henselian valuation of arbitrary rank on F with residue field κ and (char F,char κ)≠(0,2). Let ε be the unit slots of a quadratic Pfister form. Then q_ε is isotropic over F iff q_ε̄ is isotropic over κ. Equal characteristic two is included.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: The integral Pfister polynomial has nonsingular polar form modulo the maximal ideal in precisely the stated characteristic profiles. A nonzero residual zero has a nonzero polar partial derivative; a multivariable simple-root Hensel argument lifts it.
For the converse, divide an isotropic vector by a coordinate of minimum value among its finitely many coordinates. Its primitive reduction remains nonzero and isotropic.
acceptance: No rank-one, completeness, finite generation or finite residue field assumption.
Mixed characteristic (0,2) is excluded; equicharacteristic (2,2) is allowed.

nodes.title: Independent-value Pfister anisotropy
nodes.statement: Under the unit-reduction hypotheses let π₁,…,π_s∈F× have F₂-linearly independent images w(π_i) in Γ/2Γ. Then q_ε̄ over κ, q_ε over F, and q_(π,ε) over F are isotropic simultaneously. The empty π-list is allowed.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: For anisotropic residual q_ε̄, every nonzero block vector x has w(q_ε(x))=2 min_j w(x_j), by normalizing to a primitive vector.

Expand the outer tensor as the orthogonal sum over subsets χ with coefficients (−1)^|χ| π^χ. The nonzero block values belong to pairwise distinct cosets modulo 2Γ, hence attain a unique minimum and cannot cancel.
The reverse implication follows by inserting an isotropic vector into one block, together with unit reduction. The printed omission of signs is recorded in sourceIssues.
acceptance: The argument uses only finitely many blocks and works for any ordered value group.
Independence is in Γ/2Γ, not Γ⊗Q.

nodes.title: C_i fields
nodes.statement: For i≥0, a field F is C_i if every homogeneous polynomial of positive degree d in N>d^i variables has a nonzero zero over F. Zero polynomials count as homogeneous; degree zero is excluded. This is a property of actual polynomial evaluation, not a packaged existence assumption for quadratic forms only.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: Use the existing multivariate polynomial carrier and homogeneous predicate with the strict numerical bound.

Monotonicity C_i⇒C_j for i≤j follows from d≥1. Characterize C_0 by algebraic closedness using homogenized one-variable equations in one direction; in the other, restrict a homogeneous form in at least two variables to a coordinate plane and use a root of the resulting binary form over the algebraically closed field.
acceptance: The threshold is strict and degree positive.

nodes.title: The C_i theorem for systems of forms
nodes.statement: If F is C_i and f₁,…,f_r are homogeneous of the same positive degree d in N>r d^i variables, they have a common nonzero zero.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: If F is not algebraically closed, finite extensions provide anisotropic normic forms of some degree >1; compose them to obtain arbitrarily large degrees.
Pack copies of the system into a normic form. Iteration gives degrees d_j and variable counts N_j; the strict inequality N>r d^i forces N_j/d_j^i to grow until the C_i hypothesis supplies a zero.

Choose the first such zero. Anisotropy of the outer normic form forces the desired common zero. For algebraically closed F use the projective dimension theorem, and handle linear systems by linear algebra.

nodes.title: Finite Kronecker dimension and valuation drop
nodes.statement: For a field of finite absolute transcendence degree t, define δ(F)=t in positive characteristic and δ(F)=t+1 in characteristic zero. Prove δ(κ(w))<δ(F) for every nontrivial valuation w of such F. The relative algebraic closure of the prime field is called the constant field and has δ 0 or 1, respectively.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: For w trivial on the prime field lift a residue transcendence basis and adjoin an element with nonzero value. A polynomial relation is impossible by taking a term with unique smallest value; hence trdegκ+1≤trdegF.

If the residue characteristic changes from 0 to p, normalize integer coefficients by their smallest p-adic value. Reduction proves that lifted residue-independent elements are algebraically independent over Q, so trdegκ≤trdegF; the extra +1 in δ(F) gives strictness.
Algebraic extensions of the prime field and their valuations account for the constant subfield; no finite generation is assumed.

nodes.title: Finite descent of the real-place condition
nodes.statement: Let F,w be equicharacteristic-zero henselian of finite δ(F)=r, w nontrivial, with constants k and coefficient field E. Let q_η be a length r+1 Pfister form over E obtained from unit residues. If q_η is isotropic over Fk_v for every real closure k_v of k, there exists a finitely generated E′⊂E containing η such that, for k′=E′∩k, its invariant vanishes over E′k′_v for every place v of the number field k′.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: Index by finitely generated subfields E′ containing η. Nonreal places contribute zero by the local cohomological bound since δ(E′)≤δ(E)<r.

For each E′ let Σ_E′ be the finite set of real places of k′ where the invariant is nonzero. If E′⊂E″, restriction of a bad real place of k″ is a bad place of k′, since the corresponding classes restrict compatibly; this defines Σ_E″→Σ_E′. If all sets were nonempty, the finite inverse-system theorem gives a coherent real ordering of the union k.
Extend w to Fk_v. The residue field is κk_v and Ek_v is a coefficient field. Unit reduction and the assumed isotropy over Fk_v give zero invariant over Ek_v.

Along that coherent real place the fields E′k′_v form a directed union Ek_v and the invariant classes are compatible. Étale cohomological continuity says their zero image over Ek_v is zero at some later finite stage. That stage still lies in its bad-place set, a contradiction. Thus some Σ_E′ is empty, and the nonreal bounds handle all remaining places.
acceptance: The inverse-limit objects are finite sets of bad places, not Harrison spaces of all orderings.
The composita and real closures are chosen compatibly; changing the choices transports the statement by field isomorphisms.

nodes.title: The finite-dimensional unit Pfister theorem
nodes.statement: Let F have finite δ(F)=r and let w be nontrivial non-dyadic henselian, with no finite-generation hypothesis on F. Let ε be r+1 unit slots. If q_ε is isotropic over Fk_v for every real closure k_v of the constant field k, then q_ε is isotropic over F. The hypothesis is vacuous when k has no ordering.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: Positive residue characteristic is already proved in Q2.5. In residue characteristic zero replace q_ε by the coefficient-field form q_η and choose E′ by finite real-place descent.

Choose a finite transcendence basis of F/E′ and put F′=E′(T)⊂F. Then F′ is finitely generated, δ(F′)=r, and its algebraic constant field k′ is a number field. The local vanishing over E′k′_v implies local vanishing over F′k′_v.

Apply the precisely requested Jannsen local–global injectivity in H^(r+1)(F′,Z/2(r)), not an unconditional arbitrary-characteristic Hasse principle. The invariant is zero over F′, so the invariant-zero criterion and extension to F prove isotropy.
acceptance: The use of the Hasse principle occurs only in characteristic zero.
The theorem includes arbitrary algebraic and non-finitely-generated extensions of finite-transcendence-degree fields.

nodes.title: Patch openness of henselization embedding loci
nodes.statement: On Val_F=Spv(F), using the imported patch topology on valuation equivalence classes, let F_w^h denote a henselization. For every finite E/F, the locus of w admitting an F-embedding E→F_w^h is patch open. This is independent of the chosen henselization; a nonempty locus implies E/F separable.
hypotheses: F is a field; all quadratic spaces are finite-dimensional. All-characteristic statements impose no invertibility of 2.
proofSteps: A finite extension inside a henselization has an integral primitive presentation with derivative a unit, using the étale description of henselization. This is a special generator, not an arbitrary primitive element.

At such w approximate its residue by x∈F; immediate residue extension suffices. For its monic minimal polynomial p impose v(a_i)≥0, v(p(x))>0 and v(p′(x))=0. These are finitely many patch clopen conditions from Spv(F).
Every valuation in this neighborhood has a simple Hensel root of p, giving the required embedding. Union over witnesses proves openness. An inseparable E has the empty locus.
acceptance: Use the existing valuation-spectrum quotient and topology.
Only openness is asserted for the full union; individual witness neighborhoods are clopen.

checked.note: Corrected the nonsingularity locator to EKM7.19, pp.43–44; checked the mixed term, polar determinant, even-dimensional Nondegenerate convention and characteristic-two tests.

Corrected the source page to EKM p.42. The coordinate-polynomial construction is independent of basis and preserves the polar form in characteristic two; identity/tower and sum compatibility are specified.
Verified EKM8.5–8.7 and the parent Layer1 boundary. Only the characteristic-two extension is new; nonsingularity and the xy hyperbolic convention are retained.
Verified EKM §§1–4: the quotient is by metabolic symmetric bilinear forms, with tensor multiplication and dimension parity. The odd-characteristic ring is imported.
Verified EKM8.16–8.18: bilinear tensors act on the quadratic Witt group, metabolic/hyperbolic inputs vanish, and equal dimension upgrades Witt equality to isometry.
Verified the exponent shift I_b^(n−1)I_q and agreement with the imported odd-characteristic powers. The n=1 and scalar-extension tests rule out an artificial characteristic-two quadratic ring.
Verified EKM9.4 and §9B, with the current parent Pfister API. Outer factors are bilinear, the last characteristic-two slot may be zero, and only n>1 has unscaled additive generation.
Verified the quadratic étale norm and its split case. Multiplication by an invertible represented element gives the similarity, and representation of 1 gives the converse.

Made the isotropic-round case explicit: it is universal, roundness gives every similarity factor, and ρ⊥−aρ is hyperbolic without assuming ρ itself hyperbolic. Updated the acceptance test to match EKM9.8, p.54.
Verified the induction from quadratic norm forms through the binary tensor theorem. The existing low-length odd-characteristic declarations are imported.
Verified the isotropic/hyperbolic/Witt-zero/maximal-index equivalences for Pfister forms, including characteristic two. No equivalence is claimed for general isotropic forms.
Corrected EKM7.15 to p.43 and specified the highest-nonzero-coefficient argument after clearing denominators; Witt injectivity follows from anisotropic representatives.

Specified that the constrained version starts with one rational vector whose value and fixed polar pairing are both polynomial. The remainder is polar-orthogonal to the fixed vector, so reflection preserves both.

Specified binary blocks and the diagonal polar-radical remainder, and alignment by reflection in x−y. This avoids applying a regular-subspace extension theorem to a potentially singular polar complement; added exact normal-form/reflection locators.

Replaced a duplicate quadratic constructor by current QuadraticMap.scharlauTransfer and added parent Layer9. Kept the new bilinear counterpart and characteristic-two Witt-module descent, with a nonzero functional rather than a possibly zero inseparable trace.

Replaced the abbreviated proof by primitive polynomial coordinates and a smaller odd-degree irreducible factor. The argument includes inseparable extensions; removed the unnecessary Cassels–Pfister prerequisite.
Verified EKM20.14. Transfer proves the simple-extension case; parity of the remaining degree and odd-degree Witt injectivity handle arbitrary finite extensions.
Retained the unit in f=uπ after removing squares and explained the residue anisotropic-complement parity argument over the henselized DVR. The unit may be absorbed into the uniformizer.
Made the scalar existential quantifier explicit and supplied EKM20.16’s multivariable leading-coefficient induction, using odd-divisor necessity and purely transcendental Witt injectivity.
Verified the projective degree-zero fraction field, not the full cone fraction field; checked the anisotropic binary case F₂→F₄ and the dimension/transcendence-degree tests.
Verified the scaled subform conclusion for all represented units a,b, the anisotropy hypotheses and the injective-isometry convention against EKM22.5.
Verified EKM23.7, p.100: the strict dimension bound gives hyperbolicity and the nonzero anisotropic version gives dimension at least 2^n in every characteristic.
Verified Dittmann–Pop §2 and EKM §101: twist n−1, characteristic-two H¹ of logarithmic forms and Artin–Schreier degree one. The precise logarithmic coefficient extension remains requested from HL.2.
Verified Morel’s Pfister-symbol map, Steinberg relation, multiplicativity and surjectivity. Injectivity is separately planned, and the existing odd-characteristic Witt/Pfister objects are reused.

Verified the exact statement and symbol in EKM16.1/Fact16.2, pp.67–68. The unaudited primary kernel proof remains G1; BGK does not replace that proof.

Verified Dittmann–Pop3.2(1) for arbitrary-rank henselian valuations, retaining the exclusion of mixed characteristic (0,2) and inclusion of equal characteristic two.

Verified the pinned Chevalley–Warning statement suffices: the origin cannot be the sole zero when the characteristic divides the zero count.
Verified EKM97.1–97.2’s normic packing argument and N>r d^i threshold. The algebraically closed case explicitly requests the projective dimension theorem.
Verified the finite-extension descent and the reduction of an arbitrary algebraic extension to the finitely many coefficients of a polynomial. No finite-generation hypothesis is introduced.
